science.title: Manchester researchers win grant to uncover water’s unusual electrical behavior in atom-thin channels
science.description: Researchers at the National Graphene Institute (NGI) at The University of Manchester have been awarded a £1.2 million (about US$1.6 million) Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC) Standard Research Grant to investigate the electrical properties of water and aqueous electrolytes confined to spaces just a few atoms thick. The three-year project, led by Dr. Laura Fumagalli, also involves Politecnico di Milano, the University of Cambridge and Oxford Instruments Asylum Research. The Manchester team includes co-investigators Professor Sir Andre Geim and Dr. Alessandro Principi.Water plays a part in processes from energy storage and electrochemistry to biological function, yet many of its electrical properties remain poorly understood, particularly near surfaces and under extreme confinement. Measuring them directly at the atomic scale has been a major experimental challenge. The project builds on the team’s earlier work, which developed a platform for confining water inside atomically thin channels and probing its electrical behavior with nanoscale precision. Those studies found that water confined to layers only one to two nanometers thick can show unusual electrical polarizability and exceptionally high conductivity compared with bulk water. The new work will develop devices made from two-dimensional materials that can confine water and electrolytes in such channels. Using scanning dielectric microscopy, the team will map properties including conductivity and dielectric response at high spatial resolution. The project will also develop theoretical models to explain how water and ions behave under confinement, and provide experimental benchmarks for simulations in physical chemistry, electrochemistry and molecular science.“Our previous research revealed unexpected electrical properties that challenge conventional understanding,” said Fumagalli. “This new project will allow us to investigate the origins of these behaviors and explore how they change in the presence of dissolved ions and under even stronger confinement.”Water and electrolytes confined in nanoporous materials are central to batteries, fuel cells, supercapacitors, filtration membranes and iontronic devices, which use ions rather than electrons to process and transmit signals. A better understanding of their behavior could help guide developments in energy technologies, water treatment, sensing and nanofluidic systems.
